cards.title: Set Up Free Hosting, Domain and WordPress for a WooCommerce Store
cards.summary: End-to-end baseline setup: buy shared hosting, claim the free domain, install WordPress and pick the server region closest to your buying audience.
cards.use_when: Launching a brand-new store from scratch and you need hosting, a domain and WordPress installed before any product work can start.
steps: Buy a hosting plan that includes a free domain for the first year and free domain privacy; the source's example tier allowed roughly 50 sites on NVMe storage with daily backups at a promotional rate when paid for a long term (the presenter notes longer terms lower the monthly price, and later upgrades are always possible).
Register with an email and password, complete billing, and pay with whatever local method is offered; corporate/company billing fields may remove VAT charges depending on your country.
In the hosting onboarding choose: website for yourself or your business → create a new website → WordPress → set your admin email and password → create a blank website (skip AI/theme preview).
Claim the free domain at the checkout step (choose .com or a local extension), complete registrant details, and confirm via the verification email.
When asked for the target audience location, choose the server region closest to your focused buyers; the source still notes CDN keeps load times fast globally.

Expect the real domain to activate in ~10 minutes (rarely up to 24 hours); meanwhile the site loads on a temporary domain. Once active, log into the WordPress dashboard (backend) and view the front end.
caveats: Exact plan names, prices, promo codes and storage figures change; verify the current hosting interface before buying.
Domain privacy and free-domain-for-a-year offers are provider-specific, not universal.

cards.title: Clean a Fresh WordPress Install Before Building the Store
cards.summary: Remove default plugins, pages, posts and themes so the dashboard stays uncluttered and only the tools you actually need remain.
cards.use_when: Right after a fresh WordPress install, before installing WooCommerce, themes or page builders.
steps: Dismiss the dashboard welcome notice and open Screen Options to switch off the widget panels you don't use, so the dashboard is scannable.
Go to Plugins, select all, Bulk Actions → Deactivate, apply, then select all again → Delete, apply; this removes preinstalled tools such as caching plugins you may not need.
Go to Pages, select all, Move to Trash, then empty the trash; do the same for the default post under Posts.
Go to Appearance → Themes, open Theme Details on every inactive theme and Delete it, leaving exactly one theme.

Edit your profile: set first name, last name and nickname, choose the display name shown publicly on posts, pick an admin color scheme, and set the admin color scheme/display name — this is what shows as 'Howdy [name]' and authors blog posts.
Optionally register the profile email at Gravatar (free) so an avatar appears next to your author name site-wide.
Under Settings → General set site language, time zone, date format, time format and first day of week, then save.
caveats: Deleting default plugins can remove a built-in caching layer; add a caching plugin later if you need one.
Profile display name becomes public author byline — choose it deliberately.

cards.title: Write a Site Title That Matches What Buyers Search
cards.summary: Name the store around the products and markets people actually search for, not around a generic welcome phrase.
cards.use_when: Setting the WordPress site title and tagline for a new store, or rewriting them when organic/paid traffic lands on generic pages.
steps: Never use a generic site title like 'my website' or a welcome phrase; customers search for the thing they want to buy, not for your store's existence.

Check what competitors in your niche put in their titles and descriptions (e.g. searching 'buy PS5 online' surfaces titles like 'PlayStation 5, PS5, buy online'), then describe your store the same concrete way.
Optionally prompt an AI assistant with a plain description ('my website is about selling furniture, mostly sofas, in the USA and Canada — write me a great site title') and adapt the output.
Order the words so the searchable product/category terms come first and your brand name last.
Use the tagline to state a concrete service promise (the source's example: 'we deliver in the USA and Canada'), keeping it consistent with the title.
caveats: The source treats title wording as a discoverability aid, not a ranking guarantee; rankings depend on far more than the title.

cards.title: Install a Free Store Theme and Import a Starter Site
cards.summary: Use a free multipurpose theme with importable ecommerce starter sites to get product pages, categories and pages styled in minutes.
cards.use_when: Choosing the visual foundation of a new WooCommerce store when you want a working layout fast instead of designing pages from scratch.
steps: Install a free theme from Appearance → Themes → Add New by name (the source uses Blocksy), then activate it and install its companion plugin when prompted.
Delete the previously active default theme afterwards to keep the theme list to one.
Open the theme's starter-sites screen, filter to Free plans, then filter category to e-commerce.
Preview each candidate template (open several, review them, then close the ones you reject) and pick one whose product presentation you actually like.

Import it: choose the editor variant offered (the source supports Gutenberg and Elementor but notes some front-end effects such as hover zoom are missing in the Elementor variant) and select Gutenberg if you want the full set.
If WooCommerce is not yet installed it will be installed by the import; otherwise it is greyed out. Finish the import and view the site.
Inspect a demo product page: breadcrumb, title, price, short description, add-to-cart, additional information tab, and related products should already be in place.
caveats: Imported demo content includes placeholder products, images and copy — you must replace all of it before launch.
Elementor vs Gutenberg variants differ in available features; decide before importing.

cards.title: Install WooCommerce Manually and Complete the Setup Wizard
cards.summary: Add WooCommerce from the plugin repository and answer the onboarding questions so currency, industry and store address are correct.
cards.use_when: Building the store without importing a starter site, or when you need to re-run the WooCommerce setup wizard after import.
steps: Go to Plugins → Add New, search WooCommerce, install and activate; the source notes it has millions of active installs, recent updates and is maintained by the WordPress makers.
Check the 'set up my store' box after activation to enter the onboarding wizard.
Choose 'I'm just starting my business' (or the appropriate alternative) and continue.
Select your industry and the store's physical location; the country selection sets the store currency (choosing United States gives dollars).
Enter your email address, continue, and skip steps you can configure later.
Afterwards, verify the front end now shows Cart, Checkout, My Account and Shop pages — note WooCommerce places the store in 'coming soon' mode by default.
Clean the dashboard of the leftover WooCommerce setup panel via Screen Options once done.
caveats: Changing store country later affects currency, tax and shipping defaults; set it correctly up front.
The wizard wording and steps change between WooCommerce versions — verify the current wizard.

cards.title: Apply Global Brand Colors and a Logo Through the Customizer
cards.summary: Change the palette once in global color settings and have it propagate across the whole storefront, instead of editing each page.
cards.use_when: Rebranding an imported store template, adjusting colors for a client, or setting a logo/favicon before content launch.
steps: Open Appearance → Customize and locate the theme's global color settings; the source's theme exposes six palette slots used consistently across the site.
Set slot 1 (the primary/accent color used in buttons and highlights) to your brand color and watch every instance update live — this replaces manual per-element edits.
Fill the remaining slots with derived tints/shades of the same family (paste a color, drag the slider for a lighter or darker tint) so hover states and backgrounds stay coherent.

For the logo: upload an SVG where possible for sharpness and small file size (the source's example logo was about 4 KB), then set logo height (around 35 px in the example) and add the alt text and description.
Set the site icon (favicon) under Site Identity: a square image with transparent background, uploaded and cropped as needed — this shows in browser tabs and helps visitors recognise the site.

Publish and check the front end; if a section background looks off (e.g. mismatched grey vs the new accent), open the page in the block editor, select the block, and set the background to the global color or to a custom color.
caveats: Global palette slots and their names are theme-specific; a different theme may not expose the same six colors.
The source recommends SVG logos but some themes/headers may not accept SVG — test before committing.

cards.title: Shape the Header and Main Menu for Store Navigation
cards.summary: Trim and reorder the main menu, remove redundant entries, and style it to keep the sticky header usable on any page.
cards.use_when: Configuring site navigation right after importing a theme, especially before adding many product categories.
steps: Open Appearance → Customize → Menus → Main Menu and delete entries that don't belong, e.g. a 'Home' item, because the logo already links home (this mirrors how large retailer sites behave).
Drag items to reorder; drag an item slightly to the right to nest it as a sub-item under its parent (so hovering 'Products' reveals children).
Choose the menu style variant that fits (the source preferred a simple hover colour-change style over more elaborate animated styles).
Reduce excessive spacing between menu items, roughly 30 px in the source's example, to keep the header compact.
Set the menu link font colour to a darker palette slot and the hover colour to your accent slot; do the same for the header search icon and other header icons.

In header settings, choose the icon set, optionally give the header a background colour, reduce header height, and enable 'sticky' if you want the header to remain visible while scrolling (transparency is also available).
Set the header defined as the global header so the same header appears on every page; publish and verify.
caveats: Sticky headers consume vertical space on mobile; test on a phone before keeping it.
Menu style names (Type 1–4) are theme-specific.

cards.title: Standardise Layout Widths for Store and Product Pages
cards.summary: Set a container width and a narrow single-product layout so product pages read comfortably on desktop.
cards.use_when: Imported template pages feel too wide or cramped and you want a consistent grid across shop, category and product pages.
steps: In the customizer, open the global Layout section and set the site container width to about 1120 px — the source calls this a reliable default for most sites.
Then open the WooCommerce → Single Product section in the customizer and switch the single product layout to the narrower width.
Close the customizer and inspect a live product page: images, add-to-cart and description should no longer stretch edge to edge.
Re-check the shop archive and category pages to confirm the grid still looks balanced at the new container width.
caveats: 1120 px is a source-specific heuristic, not a benchmark; very image-heavy or editorial stores may need a wider container.
Option names vary by theme.

cards.title: Create a Simple Product with Price, Sale Price, Stock and Categories
cards.summary: Configure a single-option product fully: description, short description, pricing, SKU, inventory, back-order policy, purchase note, images, categories and tags.
cards.use_when: Adding a physical product that has no size/colour variants — e.g. a couch, glasses, a cap — and you need the PDP to be complete before launch.
steps: Create the product with just a name and publish to see the bare PDP, then go back and fill it in progressively.
Add a long description (appears below the fold) and a short description (appears next to the price) — they serve different positions on the product page.
Under Product data keep type 'Simple'; leave Virtual and Downloadable unchecked for physical goods.

Set the regular price and, if running a promotion, a sale price; enter sale dates so the regular price returns automatically after the end date (the source sets a sale ending the last day of the month).

Under Inventory set a SKU (useful to search stock across variants), enable stock management, enter quantity, and choose the back-order policy: disallow (safest), allow but notify customers when restocked, or allow silently — the source warns silent back-orders only work if you can restock fast.
Set a low-stock threshold (e.g. notify at two remaining) and optionally enable 'sold individually' to cap one unit per order.
Under Advanced set a purchase note shown after purchase (e.g. instructions or a scheduling link for services).
Upload a featured product image (this is the thumbnail on archives) and additional gallery images; copy the title into alt text and description for each.
Assign a category (parent or sub-category, e.g. Furniture → Sofas) and tags (material, colour, style) so the breadcrumb and related filters work.
caveats: Sale prices without an end date stay discounted until you remove them — set an end date if the promotion is time-limited.
Allowing back-orders without reliable restocking creates unhappy customers.

cards.title: Build Variable Products with Attributes, Swatches and Generated Variations
cards.summary: Define size/colour attributes once, generate every combination as a variation, then bulk-edit price and stock and set per-variation images.
cards.use_when: Listing apparel or any product with multiple sizes/colours and you want customers to select options visually on the product page.
steps: Install a variation-swatches plugin (the source uses the one from Brainstorm Force) from Plugins → Add New and activate it.

Create global attributes under WooCommerce → Attributes: define one attribute per option type (e.g. Size with type 'Label', Color with type 'Color'), each with a shape (e.g. circle) and size (e.g. 36 px).

Populate each attribute's terms: for Size add XS, S, M, L, XL, 2XL, 3XL and reorder them because new terms may be added in reverse; for Color add each colour name and pick its swatch colour (you can paste an exact hex).

Create a new product, set Product data type to 'Variable', and under Attributes add each global attribute and tick only the values this product actually has (e.g. XS, M, L, XL and black, white, navy — not all terms).
Save attributes, then click 'Generate variations': the number of variations equals the product of the selected values (4 sizes × 3 colours = 12).

Use bulk actions on the variations list to toggle manage stock across all, then set a base regular price (e.g. 19.99) and adjust outliers individually (e.g. XL at 24.99) — the PDP then shows a price range.
Override stock per variation where demand differs (XS black at 3 units, L black at 10).
Assign a featured image and gallery, then open each variation and assign its own image so switching colour changes the displayed photo; the source notes this is done once and then runs automatically.
Optionally set default form values (e.g. large + navy) and, via the swatches plugin's global styling, thicken swatch borders and centre-align swatches.
caveats: With many attribute combinations the variation list becomes long and manual per-variation images are time-consuming — budget for it.
The default-selected variation should be one you actually stock and want to feature.
Swatch styling options and centring may require extra CSS depending on theme; the source uses additional CSS for centring.

cards.title: Create a Service Product That Can Only Be Bought Once
cards.summary: List a non-shippable service (e.g. a 60-minute coaching call) with virtual product type, scheduling instructions in the purchase note, and a one-per-customer rule.
cards.use_when: Selling a bookable service, consultation or session on the same storefront as physical goods.
steps: Create a new product, give it a clear name including duration (e.g. 'Coaching call — 60 minutes') and add a cover image.
Set product type to Simple and tick Virtual so no shipping is calculated.
Set the price for one unit (e.g. 2.99 in the source's example) and write both a short and long description stating what is included.
In Advanced → Purchase note, put the post-purchase action, e.g. a scheduling link customers should visit to book their slot.
Assign a Services category so the listing sits alongside physical categories.
Under Inventory enable 'Sold individually' so a customer cannot add multiple units of a single-session service to the cart — verify on the front end that repeat add-to-cart clicks don't stack.
caveats: Purchase notes are shown after payment, not before — if scheduling must be understood pre-purchase, repeat it in the description.
Virtual products skip shipping but may still trigger tax rules depending on your configuration.

cards.title: Create a Downloadable Digital Product with Unlimited Delivery
cards.summary: Sell a file (ebook, template, software) once and deliver it automatically an unlimited number of times to each buyer.
cards.use_when: Listing any non-physical deliverable where the same file serves every customer.
steps: Create a product, set type Simple, and tick both Virtual and Downloadable.
Set a regular price (the source uses 14.99 for an ebook) — for a fixed-price digital item a sale price isn't required.
In the Downloadable files section add the file: either upload it via the media library and copy the file URL into the Downloadable files field, or select an existing media item.
Set the download expiry — leave blank/never-expiring in the source's example, or set a day limit such as 365 days if you want to limit access.
Add a short description and long description, assign a category (e.g. eBooks), and publish.
Optionally enable 'Sold individually' under Inventory so one buyer cannot purchase the same download twice in one order.
Test the purchase flow end to end to confirm the delivery link works after payment.
caveats: Uploaded media URLs are guessable if unprotected — consider a download-protection setup if the file is valuable.
The source presents unlimited downloads as a benefit, but some sellers prefer expiry windows for licensing reasons.

cards.title: List an Affiliate/External Product Without Shipping or Inventory
cards.summary: Promote a third-party product through your affiliate link by using the External/Affiliate product type, so the store shows it but checkout happens on the partner's site.
cards.use_when: Monetising storefront traffic with tools, themes or services you resell via an affiliate programme.
steps: Copy your affiliate link for the partner product.
Create a new product, give it the partner's product name, and upload a product image (the source recommends fixing odd aspect ratios, e.g. resizing to a square canvas, before uploading).
Change Product data type to 'External/Affiliate' — this removes inventory and shipping fields.
Paste the affiliate link into the product URL field and set the button text (e.g. 'Buy now', 'More information', 'See plans') to match the destination's call to action.
Enter the price context (the source shows a 'from $5 per month' style price) so shoppers know the commitment before clicking.
Write a short and long description covering what the tool does and why you recommend it, assign a category (e.g. Tools), and publish.
Open the live product page and click the button to confirm the affiliate link and tracking parameters survive the round trip.
caveats: Revenue depends on the partner's commission terms and cookie window, which the store owner does not control.
The source recommends checking the image dimensions first because external products are often displayed cropped.

cards.title: Configure Currency and Store Locale in WooCommerce
cards.summary: Set currency, formatting and separators so all prices display correctly for the store's market.
cards.use_when: Right after setting the store's country, or when the store sells to a different market than its setup country.
steps: Go to WooCommerce → Settings → General.
Set the store's country selection first, because it determines the default currency (choosing United States sets dollars).
Choose the currency symbol, then the currency position (before or after the amount).
Set the thousand separator and decimal separator per your market's convention so large prices read naturally (e.g. a $1,999 couch should not appear as 1.999).
Set the number of decimal places — the source uses two.
Save and inspect a product page and a cart page to confirm prices render across the PDP, cart, checkout and any price ranges on variable products.
caveats: Changing the currency after publishing products does not convert existing prices; you must update each price manually.
Separator and decimal settings are market conventions, not universal — match your buyer's locale.

cards.title: Use the Contrast Trick to Fix Mismatched Block Backgrounds
cards.summary: When a page section's background doesn't match the surrounding design, sample the correct colour and apply it in the block editor styles panel.
cards.use_when: After importing a template, a section on the homepage or landing page has a slightly-off background that breaks visual consistency.
steps: Install/use a browser colour-picker extension (the source uses a Chrome colour picker) to sample the exact colour of the surrounding area you want to match.
Copy the hex value.
Open the page you want to change via Edit Page (the source uses the Gutenberg block editor).
Select the section/block, open the Styles panel on the right, and choose Background.
Either pick one of the theme's global colour variations or choose Custom colour and paste the sampled hex.
Consider leaving the section transparent instead of filling it, which the source found looked better in their example.
Save and compare the rendered page against the adjacent sections.
caveats: Only applies to editors that expose a styles/background panel (e.g. Gutenberg); block or theme differences may move the option.
Sampling the wrong region compounds the mismatch — sample from the area you want to match, not from the broken section.

cards.title: Set Up Manual US State Tax Rates with Inclusive/Exclusive Display
cards.summary: Enter per-state tax percentages manually and decide whether shop prices show excluding tax while checkout shows tax inclusive.
cards.use_when: Selling to US customers where you must charge state-level sales tax, especially in a B2B/B2C hybrid store.
steps: Research the correct state and local rate for each destination you charge (the source derives exact rates, e.g. 7.2500, from TaxJar).
In WooCommerce, go to Tax → Standard Rates and insert a new row per jurisdiction.
Set the country code (e.g. US) and the state code (e.g. CA, NV) for each row, then enter the rate to four decimal places (e.g. 7.2500).
Repeat for each state you ship to, rather than applying one blanket rate.
Decide whether standard, reduced and zero rates are needed — reduced for categories like books, zero for digital products.

For hybrid B2B/B2C stores, configure prices to display excluding tax in the shop/catalogue but inclusive at checkout so B2B buyers can see the net figure while consumers see the final amount they pay.
Test the cart and checkout with an address in each configured state to confirm the rate applies and the display mode behaves as intended.
caveats: The source notes exact US state rates should come from a tax service rather than being guessed — many states have local district taxes on top of the state rate.
Displaying net prices in the shop while charging gross at checkout can surprise consumers; check this matches your market's legal expectations.
Tax rules and WooCommerce tax screens have changed across versions — verify the current settings UI.

cards.title: Set Shipping Cost Brackets and a Free-Shipping Threshold in WooCommerce
cards.summary: Use a shipping plugin's conditions to charge by cart-price bracket and unlock free shipping above a threshold.
cards.use_when: Configuring shipping zones and rates for a physical-goods store where you want shipping cost to scale with order value.
steps: Install a WooCommerce shipping plugin that supports conditions based on cart totals or price brackets.
Define brackets mapping cart value to cost — the source's examples include $0–$90 costing $6.99 and a $20–$49 bracket costing $8.99.
Add a free-shipping condition for carts above your chosen threshold (the source uses $200).
Review the brackets for gaps or overlaps before saving; a customer's cart value must land in exactly one bracket.
Test the cart at several price points — just under and just over the free-shipping threshold, and inside each bracket — to confirm the correct rate appears.
Check that variable and sale-priced products still produce the same bracket logic at checkout.
caveats: Bracket values and the free-shipping threshold are source-specific examples, not recommended numbers — set them from your own margin analysis.
Plugin conditions vary: some evaluate cart subtotal before tax/discounts, others after, which changes which bracket applies.
